                              OFFICE OF PUBLIC UTILITY COUNSEL'S
                                  POST-HEARING INITIAL BRIEF

        The Office of Public Utility Counsel (OPUC), representing the interests of residential and

small commercial consumers in Texas, respectfully files this post-hearing initial brief in response

to the State Office of Administrative Hearings' (SOAH) Order Nos. 6 and 32. Pursuant to the

Orders, the deadline for the parties to file post-hearing initial briefs is June 19,2026.1 Therefore,

this brief is timely filed.

                                          I.      RESPONSE

        This proceeding to resolve Oncor Electric Delivery Company LLC' s (Oncor) and LCRA

Transmission Service Corporation's (LCRA) (collectively, Applicants) Certificate of Convenience

and Necessity (CCN) amendment application for the Bell County East Switch to Big Hill




        1 SOAH Order No. 6 - Memorializing Prehearing Conference; Granting Good-Cause Exception; Extending
Comment Deadline on Application and Notice; Adopting Schedule; Setting Route Adequacy & Merits Hearings;
Addressing Procedures Advising Intervenors on Dismissal at 7 (Apr. 20,2026); SOAH Order No. 32 - Addressing
Post-Hearing Matters (Jun. 15, 2026).


                                                     1
 Substation 765 kilovolt (kV) transmission line (Project) involves multitudes of unrepresented

parties, including landowners or groups of landowners that would be adversely affected by the

construction of a transmission line on or in the proximity of their properties.2 In addition to the

hundreds of unrepresented parties that were admitted to this proceeding, hundreds more were

stricken. 3

        The Administrative Law Judges' (ALJs) handling of this proceeding deserves

commendation. While the quantity of stricken intervenors reflects a need for process

improvements on the front end, the ALJs performed admirably during this proceeding in allowing

unrepresented parties to participate as fully and meaningfully as possible under this extremely

compressed timeline that disproportionately burdened all intervenors to this docket.

        Inevitably, some landowners will be adversely impacted by the construction of this

transmission line. Therefore, the ALJs and the Public Utility Commission of Texas (Commission)

should scrutinize this application with the aim of having the fewest number of landowners,

particularly residential and small commercial consumers, affected by approval of this project.

Rather than take a position on a specific route, OPUC would like to assist the ALJs and the

Commission with an outline of the law and a summary of some facts the Commission has

considered in past transmission line CCN dockets.

        This application is subject to the statutory requirements in Public Utility Regulatory Act

(PURA) § 37.056 and Commission's rules found in 16 Tex. Admin. Code (TAC) § 25.101(b)(3).

The Commission may grant a CCN request only if it finds that "the certificate is necessary for the

 service, accommodation, convenience, or safety of the public."4 The Applicants bear the burden

of demonstrating the necessity of their proposed CCNs.5 After considering the adequacy of

existing service, the need for additional service, and the effect of granting the certificate on the

applicant and any electric utility serving the surrounding territory, the Commission may grant the

CCN.6 In a prior order, the Commission reaffirmed the applicants' need to meet these requirements

established in PURA § 37.056(a).7


         The Commission is also required to consider the following factors in approving or denying

a CCN request: "(A) community values; (B) recreational and park areas; (C) historical and

aesthetic values; (D) environmental integrity; and (E) the probable improvement qf service or

lowering of cost to consumers in the area if the cerlificate is granted                       „ 8 These " factors are

stated in the broadest possible terms and are intended as legislative standards to guide the

Commission in its administration of the certification process."' The Commission is required to

consider the factors only in the context of the case at hand. 10 These factors give the Commission

stated objectives to work towards, and some ofthe factors may compete. 11 Thus, "the Commission

         To ensure the fewest number of residential and small commercial customers are impacted,

the Commission should heavily weigh PURA § 37.056(a)(4)(E). Subsection (IF) should be given

greater weight when evaluating the Proj ect because residential and small commercial ratepayers

are not the source ofthese requested improvements. This application will not immediately impact

customers' bills, but the costs to construct the Project will eventually be borne by ratepayers when

included in rates in a subsequent Transmission Cost of Service or comprehensive rate proceeding.

Once the costs are established in this CCN proceeding, they will be passed down to residential and

small commercial consumers without the lowering of costs contemplated in subsection (E). Thus,

assuming that the construction of this line would probably improve the service to customers in the

Applicants' service areas, it is imperative that the selected route be the most cost-effective to all

ratepayers with the smallest impact to residential and small commercial consumers.

         That being said, none of the statutory factors are intended to be absolute in the sense that

any one factor shall prevail in all possible circumstances. 13 The other factors listed in subsections

(A)-(D) should be weighed from the perspective of those most significantly impacted by the

proposed routes: the Texans that live there. The Legislature has underscored the critical importance

of the interests of local Texans by requiring the Commission to evaluate how approval of a CCN

application would affect community values. 14 The term "community values" is not formally

Util. Comm 'n v . Texland Elec. Co., 101 S . W . 2d 261 , 267 ( Tex . App .- Austin 1985 )).
          14 See PURA § 37.056 (c)(4)(A) ("The commission shall grant each certificate on a nondiscriminatory basis
[onlyl after considering   community values") [emphasis added].

 defined by statute or Commission rules. However, in several CCN dockets the Commission and

Commission Staff have recognized a working definition as "a shared appreciation of an area or

other mutual resource by a national, regional, or local community." 15 The Commission has further

found that "[aldverse effects upon community values consist ofthose aspects of a proposed project

that would significantly alter the use, enj oyment, or intrinsic value attached to an important area

or resource by a community."16

        The Applicants propose 122 alternative routes and 171 alternative route links with a total

line length of between 214 and 244 miles. 17 The study area in this proceeding encompasses

portions of 15 counties which contain commercial, residential, and industrial development as well

as Fort Hood. 18 At the hearing on the merits, testimony was admitted from the residents who

would be directly affected by this project that addressed topics they deemed important to the

factors outlined in PURA § 37.056(a)(4)(A)-(D) and 16 TAC § 25.101(b)(3)(B). No party would

contest that their concerns such as impact to property values, limitation on land use, preservation

of recreational and culturally significant locations, and potential health impacts were fervently

discussed.

        The Commission and the ALJs should give those concerns raised by pro se parties in the

case equal footing to those raised by represented parties. This project will have long-term impacts

not be disregarded simply because they could not meet the cumbersome procedural requirements

to have their individual voice heard. This is especially true considering the condensed timeline

driven by the statutory deadline for a final Commission determination.

         Applicants for a transmission line CCN must route the line to the extent reasonable to

moderate the impact to landowners and the local community.19 When addressing recreational and

park areas, the Commission has previously found that routing lines along property boundaries or

fencelines when possible while avoiding habitable structures and recreational areas has helped

preserve community values and recreational areas.20 This aligns with the Commission's rule

addressing prudent avoidance, 21 which is achieved by minimizing the number of habitable

structures located in close proximity to the routes in order to minimize exposure to electric and

magnetic fields (EMF).22 In the past, the Commission has additionally ordered the implementation

of "optimum phasing" to reduce the impact ofEMF.23 However, the Commission should be aware

that prudent avoidance and the general desirability of paralleling24 may conflict in certain

reliability risks due to an interaction of magnetic fields between the lines known as "mutual

         The Commission has defined aesthetics so as "to accommodate the subjective perception

of natural beauty in a landscape and measure an area' s scenic qualities.',26 The Commission has

determined that "[alesthetic impacts or impacts to visual resources exist when the [right-of-wayl,

lines, or structures of a transmission-line system individually or in combination create an intrusion

into, or substantially alter, the character of the existing view.',27 The Commission has considered

both the temporary impacts such as construction and clearing as well as permanent impacts due to

the view impact of the completed structures and lines when assessing aesthetic effects. 28 The

significance of such impacts is "directly related to the quality of the view in natural scenic areas,

the importance ofthe existing setting in the use or enj oyment of an area, and in valued community

resources in recreational areas."29

impact of transmission line projects such as minimizing right-of-way clearing, reclaiming

construction sites with native species, using only selective clearing techniques, and prohibiting use

of chemical herbicides for controlling vegetation within the right-of-way in environmentally

sensitive areas and near streams.32

           II.      CONSIDERATION OF NON-UNIFORM LANDOWNER INPUT

        During the hearing, several intervenors complained of difficulties with notice and

opportunities to participate prior to the hearing. While OPUC does not assert that the Applicants

failed to comply with any rule or law, OPUC would draw the ALJ' s attention to the rebuttal

testimony of Casey Petty. In his rebuttal, Petty acknowledges that certain persons were not given

notice of public participation meetings because no preliminary routes ran within 520 feet of their

properties. 33 He continues that after such meetings were held, as a result of route modifications,

the properties of then un-noticed persons came to be impacted. 34 The applicants did not host a

                                      III.   CONCLUSION

       For the reasons stated herein, OPUC respectfully requests that the SOAH ALJs adopt and

incorporate OPUC' s recommendations into the proposal for decision in this proceeding. OPUC

further asks to be granted any other relief to which it may be entitled.
